# References and Reading

Go from the explanation to the source, with the right version in hand.

This book separates three kinds of material: protocol specifications, implementation documentation, and original teaching examples. An example name, diagram, or latency budget is illustrative unless explicitly identified otherwise.

## The protocol baseline

The IETF baseline is [Media over QUIC Transport, draft-21](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-21), published September 8, 2026. Chapters link to relevant sections of that pinned version. Consult the [current document status](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-moq-transport/) for later revisions and the [MoQ working group](https://datatracker.ietf.org/wg/moq/about/) for the broader standards effort.

Read the object model before the wire-message tables. Once tracks and groups make sense, the fields become answers to recognizable problems rather than an arbitrary list of integers.

## The transport underneath

[RFC 9000](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000.html) defines QUIC’s transport, including streams, flow control, and cancellation. [RFC 9001](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9001.html) describes its use of TLS. [RFC 9002](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9002.html) covers loss detection and congestion control.

[RFC 9221](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9221.html) defines the QUIC DATAGRAM extension. Read it when deciding whether a small payload should be retried or replaced, and when checking message-size constraints.

## Browser interfaces

The [W3C WebTransport specification](https://www.w3.org/TR/webtransport/) describes the browser API for streams and datagrams. Its presence does not remove the need for a protocol library above it.

The [W3C WebCodecs specification](https://www.w3.org/TR/webcodecs/) describes low-level codec interfaces. It is useful for understanding decoder configuration and frame ownership. It does not define a full media player.

## The moq.dev implementation

Start with [moq.dev](https://moq.dev/) and the [concepts guide](https://doc.moq.dev/concept/). Then read the separate explanations of [moq-lite](https://doc.moq.dev/concept/moq-lite), [hang](https://doc.moq.dev/concept/hang), and [transport choices](https://doc.moq.dev/concept/transport).

For experiments, use the [setup](https://doc.moq.dev/setup/) and [development](https://doc.moq.dev/setup/dev) documentation. For a reachable relay, read the [production guide](https://doc.moq.dev/setup/prod). These pages describe a particular project and can evolve independently of this book’s IETF baseline.

## Editorial approach and limitations

Research for this edition was checked on **September 16, 2026**. The guide emphasizes stable ideas and avoids presenting a moving wire format as permanent. Draft-sensitive explanations refer to draft-21; implementation-specific examples are labeled with the project name.

This guide does not claim measured performance results, exhaustive browser compatibility, or successful execution of the upstream walkthrough. The latency values are invented examples. Validate a chosen stack and revision in your own deployment before relying on particular behavior.

[WebRTC for the Curious](https://webrtcforthecurious.com/docs/01-what-why-and-how/) inspired the concepts-first chapter structure and accessible tone. This site uses original prose and diagrams and is not an official extension of that book.

## Keeping an edition accurate

When updating the book, record the new research date and protocol revision together. Review terminology, setup, subscription behavior, timeout semantics, and the media-format boundary before changing the edition badge.

Keep examples identified as examples. If you add benchmarks, publish the workload, hardware, network conditions, implementation versions, and measurement points. If you add runnable SDK code, pin dependencies and verify it against the corresponding relay. An explanation is most useful when readers can tell exactly what it establishes.
